result:
The premise isn't right: more agents don't always give better results. So neither five nor ten is the answer yet.

It's tempting because a team of specialists sounds like it should beat one generalist. But every extra agent has a cost:
- Each agent makes its own model calls, so cost per request goes up. Anthropic's engineering team reported that multi-agent systems used many times more tokens than a single agent. That's a number to check at the source before you quote it at your design review.
- Every hand-off is a chance to lose information. One agent summarizes for the next, and a detail like "the laser cutter needs the safety training" can get dropped.
- More pieces means more to debug and explain.

**Example.** A student asks, "Can I book the 3D printer Thursday at 2?" One agent can do this. It calls the calendar tool, sees the slot is free, checks the student's training status, books it, and replies. Splitting it into a "question agent", a "calendar agent" and a "booking agent" adds two hand-offs and about three times the model calls, and it fixes nothing.

**The general idea.** Start with the simplest design that works: a fixed workflow where the steps are known, and one agent with good tools where the model has to decide what to do next. Split into several agents only when you can name the problem the split solves. Examples are work that can run in parallel, or one job that would overload another's context, such as digesting long manuals. "More is better" isn't a reason.

For your assistant, I'd start with one agent and three tools: manual search, calendar check and booking. Measure where it fails and what it costs, and split only if the data shows a reason.

Quick check: for the 3D printer request above, what's one thing a split would cost you, and what would it have to buy you to be worth it?

I can teach a full lesson on when multi-agent pays off if you want one.
